Nebuzaradan
nĕb-ū-zăr-ā'dăn
n. (captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard — the officer who burned the temple, and who set Jeremiah free with a sermon)
From Hebrew Nebuzar'adan, representing an Akkadian name meaning something like “Nabu has given seed”. His title, rab-tabbachim, is literally chief of the slaughterers — captain of the guard, the same office Potiphar held in Egypt.

Biblical Definition

Nebuzaradan is the Babylonian officer who executed the sentence on Jerusalem. He came in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (2Ki 25:8), burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and every great man's house, broke down the walls, and carried away the remnant of the people (2Ki 25:11). He is the hand on the fire. And Scripture, having established that, records two further things about him that are harder to hold. The first is his social policy: “Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, which had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time” (Jer 39:10) — the destitute of Judah received land from the invader that their own nobles had never given them. The second is his theology. Standing over Jeremiah in chains at Ramah, this heathen soldier preached Judah's own prophets back to it: “The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place” (Jer 40:2), and went on to say that it had come because they had sinned against the LORD and not obeyed His voice. Then he offered the prophet his choice: come to Babylon and be looked after, or stay. Jeremiah stayed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Nebuzaradan; in sacred history he is the captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar who destroyed Jerusalem and released Jeremiah.

expand to see more

NEBUZARADAN, n. Captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

He came against Jerusalem in the nineteenth year of that king, and burnt the house of the Lord.

He carried away the remnant of the people, leaving the poor of the land for vinedressers and husbandmen.

He took Jeremiah from among the captives at Ramah and set him at liberty, committing him to Gedaliah.

The title captain of the guard signifies in the Hebrew the chief of the executioners.

Key Scripture

2Ki 25:8 — "And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem:"

2Ki 25:11 — "Now the rest of the people that were left in the city, and the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon, with the remnant of the multitude, did Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carry away."

Jer 39:10 — "But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, which had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time."

Jer 40:2 — "And the captain of the guard took Jeremiah, and said unto him, The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place."

Modern Corruption

A pagan executioner states the covenant doctrine of the exile more plainly than the priests of Jerusalem had; the church still prefers explanations of judgment that do not name sin.

expand to see more

Jer 40:2-3 is one of the most uncomfortable speeches in the Old Testament, because of who makes it. Judah had been told for forty years by Jeremiah that the city would fall for covenant-breaking, and had answered with a state religion of reassurance — “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 6:14). Then a Babylonian officer, standing in the ashes, gives the correct interpretation of the event: the LORD your God said this would happen, He has done what He said, and it is because you sinned against Him. When the pulpit will not preach the reason for a judgment, God is perfectly capable of having it preached by a heathen with a sword.

The other thing to name is Jer 39:10, because it cuts against a comfortable assumption. The poor of Judah, who had nothing, were given vineyards and fields — by the invader. God had commanded jubilee, gleaning, and the release of debts, and Judah had ignored them until the land took its sabbaths by force. It is a sober thing when an unbelieving power does more for the destitute than the covenant community did. The dictionary rejects the framework that makes economic grievance the master category of Scripture, but it will not soften what the prophets say about a nation that grinds the faces of its poor and calls itself the people of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Nebuzar'adan (H5018), Nebuzaradan; rab-tabbachim (H7227 + H2876), chief of the guard, literally chief of the slaughterers.

expand to see more

Hebrew Nebuzar'adan (H5018) — Nebuzaradan; from the Babylonian god Nabu, as in Nebuchadnezzar and Nebushasban.

Hebrew tabbach (H2876) — a slaughterer, cook, executioner; the root of his title.

Hebrew rab-tabbachim — captain of the guard; the office Potiphar held under Pharaoh (Gen 37:36).

Hebrew dal (H1800) — the poor, the weak; those left in the land with vineyards (Jer 39:10).

Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn; what he did to the house of the LORD (2Ki 25:9).

Usage

"“Came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard” — the sentence arriving in person."

"“Left of the poor of the people, which had nothing” — land given by an invader."

"“The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place” — a heathen preaching Judah's own prophets."
